children: Investors who dumped bonds on Wednesday over growing inflation fears may have been spooked by an S&P PMI survey that paints a misleadingly hot picture of the U.S. economy, according to Pantheon Macroeconomics.

However, Pantheon Chief U.S. Economist Samuel Tombs is warning that investors have "overreacted" to the S&P data by ignoring other equally useful indicators.

The six regional Fed business surveys released so far for September "collectively present a much more restrained picture of GDP growth," Tombs wrote in a social media post. He pointed out that historically, these Fed surveys have held a slight edge in accurately tracking the economy, noting that "they did not falsely signal a recession in 2022, as the S&P PMI did."
Four more regional surveys are slated for release over the coming week, which may further balance the narrative.

Tombs also emphasized a key disconnect in the labor data, highlighting the "lack of any relationship between the employment index of S&P's survey and payrolls." According to his analysis, this discrepancy bolsters the case for treating the S&P PMI's signal of a booming economy with a heavy dose of skepticism.
